6.0.oldText: 186. Europe's moral feeling today may be as subtle, late-developed, varied, sensitive, and refined as its corresponding “Science of Morals” is new, preliminary, awkward, and clumsy. An interesting contrast, sometimes embodied quite visibly in a moralist himself. Indeed, “Science of Morals” is a far too presumptuous name for what it denotes, and offends GOOD taste, which always anticipates more modest expressions. We should honestly acknowledge WHAT will still be needed here for a long time, WHAT alone is appropriate now: collecting material, surveying and classifying the immense field of delicate feelings and distinctions of value that live, grow, reproduce, and die. Perhaps we might also try to describe the recurring, commoner forms of these living crystallisations, in preparation for a THEORY OF TYPES of morality. Until now, people have certainly not been so modest. Whenever philosophers addressed morality as a science, they demanded something much grander, more pretentious, more ceremonious of themselves, with pedantic, ridiculous solemnity. They wanted to GIVE MORALITY A FOUNDATION—and every philosopher has believed he provided one, while treating morality itself as something “given.” How remote from their clumsy pride was the apparently insignificant problem, abandoned to dust and decay, of describing the forms of morality: a task for which the finest hands and senses would scarcely be fine enough! Moral philosophers knew the moral facts only imperfectly, through an arbitrary digest or accidental selection—perhaps the morality of their own surroundings, position, church, Zeitgeist, climate, or region. Precisely because they knew so little about peoples, eras, and earlier ages, and had little desire to learn, they never even glimpsed the real problems of morality, which emerge only by comparing MANY moralities. Strange as it sounds, every “Science of Morals” so far has OMITTED the problem of morality itself. No one suspected that anything was problematic here! Properly examined, what philosophers called “giving morality a foundation” was merely a learned form of good FAITH in the prevailing morality, a fresh way of EXPRESSING it. It was therefore just another fact within a particular morality, and, in its deepest motive, a denial that questioning that morality was PERMISSIBLE—certainly the opposite of testing, analysing, doubting, and dissecting that faith. Listen to the almost admirable innocence with which Schopenhauer describes his task, and judge how scientific a “Science” can be when its latest master still speaks like children and old wives. “The principle,” he says on page 136 of the Grundprobleme der Ethik, [Footnote: Pages 54-55 of Schopenhauer's Basis of Morality, translated by Arthur B. Bullock, M.A. (1903).] “the axiom on whose meaning all moralists PRACTICALLY agree: neminem laede, immo omnes quantum potes juva—is REALLY the proposition all moral teachers seek to establish, ... the REAL foundation of ethics, sought for centuries like the philosopher's stone.” Establishing that proposition may indeed be difficult; Schopenhauer's own failure is well known. Anyone who has fully grasped its absurd falsity and sentimentality in a world whose essence is Will to Power may recall that this pessimist ACTUALLY played the flute... every day after dinner, as his biography relates. An incidental question: a pessimist who rejects God and the world but STOPS SHORT at morality, assents to it, and plays the flute to laede-neminem morals—what? Is that really a pessimist?

6.2.oldText: 188. Set against laisser-aller, every morality is a kind of tyranny over “nature” and over “reason.” But this is no objection unless we again use some morality to decree that every tyranny and irrationality is forbidden. What is essential and priceless in any morality is its prolonged constraint. To understand Stoicism, Port Royal, or Puritanism, recall the discipline through which every language gained strength and freedom: metrical constraint, the tyranny of rhyme and rhythm. What pains the poets and orators of every nation have taken! This includes some present-day prose writers, whose ears harbour an unyielding conscientiousness. “For the sake of nonsense,” say utilitarian bunglers, imagining this makes them wise; “in submission to arbitrary laws,” say anarchists, imagining this makes them “free,” even free-spirited. Yet the remarkable fact remains: everything that exists or has existed in the way of freedom, elegance, daring, dance, and masterly assurance—in thought itself, government, speech and persuasion, art as much as conduct—developed only under the tyranny of such arbitrary laws. Seriously, it is quite possible that THIS is “nature” and “natural,” rather than laisser-aller! Every artist knows how far his “most natural” state is from letting himself go: in moments of “inspiration,” freely arranging, placing, disposing, and constructing, he obeys a thousand laws with strictness and delicacy. Their very rigidity and precision defeat any attempt to formulate them in concepts; beside them even the firmest concept seems fluid, multiple, and ambiguous. The essential thing “in heaven and on earth,” apparently—to repeat it—is prolonged OBEDIENCE in one direction. In the long run this produces, and always has produced, something that makes life worth living: virtue, art, music, dance, reason, spirituality—something transfiguring, refined, foolish, or divine. The spirit's long servitude; the suspicious restrictions on communicating thoughts; the discipline thinkers imposed on themselves to follow a church's or court's rules, or Aristotelian premises; the persistent spiritual determination to read every event through a Christian scheme and rediscover and justify the Christian God in everything: all this violence, arbitrariness, harshness, terror, and irrationality trained the European spirit into its strength, relentless curiosity, and subtle agility. Admittedly, much irreplaceable strength and spirit had to be crushed, stifled, and ruined along the way. Here, as everywhere, “nature” shows herself in all her extravagant, INDIFFERENT magnificence, shocking yet noble. For centuries Europeans thought only to prove something—whereas now we distrust any thinker who “wants to prove something.” The result their most rigorous thinking WAS TO reach was fixed beforehand, as perhaps in ancient Asiatic astrology, or still today in the innocent Christian-moral interpretation of immediate personal events “for God's glory” or “for the soul's good.” This tyranny, this arbitrariness, this stern and magnificent stupidity EDUCATED the spirit. Slavery, both coarse and subtle, apparently remains indispensable even to spiritual education and discipline. Every morality can be viewed this way: “nature” within it teaches hatred of laisser-aller and excessive freedom, creates the need for restricted horizons and immediate duties, teaches the NARROWING OF PERSPECTIVES. Thus, in a sense, it teaches that stupidity is a condition of life and growth. “You must obey someone, and for a long time; OTHERWISE you will come to grief and lose all respect for yourself”: this seems to me nature's moral imperative. It is certainly not “categorical,” as old Kant wanted—hence the “otherwise”—nor is it addressed to individuals (what does nature care about an individual!), but to peoples, races, ages, and ranks, and above all to the animal “man” as a whole, to HUMANITY.

6.3.oldText: 189. Industrious peoples find idleness very hard to bear. ENGLISH instinct performed a masterstroke by making Sunday so sacred and gloomy that an Englishman unconsciously longs for the weekday and working day again. It is a cleverly devised, cleverly inserted FAST, of a kind often found in antiquity too, though, appropriately for southern peoples, not specifically a fast from work. Many kinds of fasting are needed. Wherever powerful influences and habits prevail, lawmakers must arrange intervening days when those drives are restrained and learn to hunger afresh. Seen from above, entire generations and eras infected by moral fanaticism resemble these inserted periods of restraint and fasting. A drive learns to humble and submit itself—and also to PURIFY and SHARPEN itself. 6.4.oldText: 190. Something in Plato's morality does not truly belong to Plato; it appears in his philosophy almost despite him. This is Socratism, for which he himself was too noble. “Nobody wishes to harm himself; therefore every evil deed is done unknowingly. The evil person injures himself, but would not do so if he knew that evil was evil. He is therefore evil only through error. Free him from error and you necessarily make him—good.” This reasoning smells of the POPULACE, who notice only wrongdoing's unpleasant consequences and effectively conclude, “Doing wrong is STUPID.” Without further thought they equate “good” with “useful and pleasant.” We can immediately suspect the same origin in every utilitarian system and follow the trail; we shall seldom be mistaken. Plato did everything possible to read refinement and nobility into his teacher's doctrines, and above all to read himself into them. This most daring interpreter lifted the whole Socrates out of the street like a popular tune and song, presenting him in endless, impossible variations: in all Plato's own disguises and multiplicities. Speaking playfully, and in Homeric language, what is Plato's Socrates if not — “πρόσθε Πλάτων ὄπιθεν τε Πλάτων μέσση τε Χίμαιρα” (“Plato in front, Plato behind, and in the middle a Chimaera”)?

6.5.oldText: 191. The old theological question of “Faith” and “Knowledge”—more plainly, instinct and reason—asks whether instinct should hold greater authority in evaluating things than rationality, which wants to assess and act on motives, on a “Why,” that is, according to purpose and usefulness. It is the same old moral problem that first appeared in Socrates and divided minds long before Christianity. Naturally following the inclination of his talent, that of an unsurpassed dialectician, Socrates initially sided with reason. Indeed, what did he do all his life but mock the awkward helplessness of noble Athenians, instinctive people like all nobles, who could never satisfactorily explain why they acted as they did? Ultimately, though silently and secretly, he laughed at himself as well. His finer conscience and self-examination revealed the same difficulty and incapacity within him. “But why,” he asked himself, “should that make us abandon the instincts! We must set them right, and reason TOO: follow the instincts, but persuade reason to support them with sound arguments.” This was the great, mysterious ironist's real FALSENESS. He trained his conscience to be satisfied with a kind of self-trickery; in fact, he recognised the irrationality within moral judgment. Plato, more innocent in these matters and lacking the plebeian's cunning, spent all his strength—the greatest any philosopher had ever expended—trying to prove to himself that reason and instinct spontaneously converge on the good, on “God.” Since Plato, theologians and philosophers have all followed that road. This means instinct—or what Christians call “Faith,” and I call “the herd”—has so far prevailed in morality. One might except Descartes, rationalism's father and therefore the Revolution's grandfather, who acknowledged only reason's authority. But reason is merely an instrument, and Descartes was superficial.

6.6.oldText: 192. Anyone who has traced the history of a single science will find in its development a clue to the oldest, commonest processes of all “knowledge and cognition.” There, as here, the first things to develop are premature hypotheses, fictions, the good, foolish will to “believe,” and a lack of patience and suspicion. Our senses learn late, and never completely, to become subtle, trustworthy, cautious instruments of knowledge. In any given case, the eye finds it easier to reproduce an often-produced image than to grasp what is different and new in an impression; the latter takes more strength, more “morality.” Hearing something new is difficult and painful for the ear; unfamiliar music reaches us badly. Listening to a foreign language, we automatically try to shape its sounds into words we know better. Thus Germans turned the spoken ARCUBALISTA into ARMBRUST, cross-bow. Our senses too resist and dislike novelty. Even in the “simplest” sensations, emotions generally RULE: fear, love, hatred, and the passive feeling of laziness. A modern reader scarcely reads every word on a page, much less every syllable; instead, he picks out perhaps five of every twenty words at random and “guesses” their likely meaning. In much the same way, we do not see a tree's leaves, branches, colour, and shape fully and accurately. Imagining a rough approximation of a tree is much easier. We do the same even amid the most extraordinary experiences: we invent most of the experience, and can hardly be persuaded to contemplate an event EXCEPT as its “inventors.” All this shows that, by our fundamental nature and from the remotest times, we have been ACCUSTOMED TO LYING. Or, more politely and hypocritically—in short, more pleasantly—we are far more artistic than we realise. During a lively conversation, I often see the other person's face with astonishing clarity, shaped by the thought he expresses or that I believe his mind contains. The detail exceeds my eyesight's actual POWER, so I MUST have imagined the subtle movements of muscles and expression in the eyes. Probably he wore an entirely different expression, or none at all.

Suppose someone has often flown in dreams until, whenever he dreams, he recognises the power and art of flight as his privilege, his own enviable happiness. People differ not only in their lists of desirable things—in which goods they consider worth pursuing, and in the greater or lesser value and ranking they assign to generally recognised goods. They differ much more in what they count as actually HAVING and POSSESSING something desirable. With a woman, for instance, a more modest man considers control over her body and sexual pleasure sufficient proof of ownership. Another, more suspicious and ambitious in his desire to possess, sees how questionable and merely apparent such ownership is. He wants subtler tests, particularly whether she not only gives herself to him but also gives up for him what she has or would like to have. Only THEN does he consider her “possessed.” A third man's distrust and appetite for possession do not stop even there. He wonders whether, in surrendering everything, she is perhaps surrendering to a phantom of him. He first wants to be known thoroughly, indeed profoundly; to be loved at all, he dares let himself be discovered. Only when she no longer deceives herself about him, loving his devilry and hidden insatiability as much as his goodness, patience, and spirituality, does he feel she belongs entirely to him. One man wants to possess a people and finds every higher art of Cagliostro and Catalina suited to the task. Another, with a more refined appetite, tells himself, “Where we want to possess, we must not deceive.” The thought of a mask of himself ruling the people's hearts makes him impatient and angry: “Then I must MAKE myself known, and first learn to know myself!” Helpful, charitable people almost always display a clumsy cunning: they first dress up the person they will help as someone “deserving,” seeking precisely THEIR assistance, who will respond with profound gratitude, attachment, and submission. Through these fancies they take possession of the needy, just as their charity and helpfulness generally spring from the desire to own. Interfere with their benevolence, or get there first, and they become jealous. Parents involuntarily shape their children into something resembling themselves, calling it “education.” Deep down, no mother doubts that giving birth makes the child her property; no father questions his right to HIS OWN ideas and valuations. The Jews—a people “born for slavery,” according to Tacitus and the entire ancient world, “the chosen people among the nations,” according to their own belief and declaration—performed the miracle of reversing valuations. All moral systems addressing individuals in the name of their so-called “happiness”—what are they but advice on behaviour suited to the degree of DANGER those individuals pose to themselves? Recipes for their passions, their good and bad tendencies, insofar as these possess the Will to Power and want to rule; small and large expedients and elaborations, permeated by the stale smell of family remedies and old wives' wisdom. Their form is always grotesque and absurd because they address “everyone,” generalising where no generalisation is warranted. They all speak unconditionally and take themselves unconditionally. All need more than one grain of salt: they become tolerable, sometimes even seductive, only when heavily seasoned and beginning to smell dangerously, especially of “the other world.” Intellectually considered, this has little value and is far from “science,” much less “wisdom.” Let it be repeated three times: expediency, expediency, expediency, mixed with stupidity, stupidity, stupidity.
