9.0.oldText: 240. I HEARD Richard Wagner's overture to the Mastersinger again, as though for the first time. It is a magnificent, sumptuous, heavy work of late art, proud enough to assume that two centuries of music remain alive in its listeners if they are to understand it. It honours the Germans that this pride was justified! What flavours and powers, what seasons and climates mingle here! At one moment it strikes us as ancient, at another as foreign, bitter, and too modern. It is as wilful as it is grandly traditional, often mischievous, more often rough and coarse. It has fire and courage, yet also the loose, brownish skin of fruit that ripens too late. It flows broadly and fully; suddenly an inexplicable hesitation appears, like a gap opening between cause and effect, an oppressive dreaminess, almost a nightmare. Already, though, the old stream of pleasure widens again, pleasure in its many forms, old and new happiness. ESPECIALLY present is the artist's delight in himself, which he refuses to hide: his astonished, happy awareness of mastering the devices he uses here, the new, newly acquired, incompletely tested artistic devices he seems to reveal to us. Yet taken altogether there is no beauty, no South, none of the delicate clarity of southern skies, no grace, no dance, scarcely any desire for logic. There is even a certain clumsiness, deliberately emphasized, as if the artist were saying, “It is part of my intention”. Heavy drapery, something wilfully barbaric and ceremonial, a fluttering of learned, venerable conceits and jokes: something German in the word's best and worst senses, something in the German manner, many-sided, shapeless, inexhaustible. A certain German strength and overflowing fullness of soul is unafraid to conceal itself beneath the RAFFINEMENTS of decadence, and perhaps feels most at home there. It is a true, genuine sign of the German soul, simultaneously young and old, overripe yet still too rich in possibilities for the future. This music best expresses what I think of the Germans: they belong to the day before yesterday and the day after tomorrow—THEY HAVE NO TODAY YET.

9.1.oldText: 241. We “good Europeans” also have hours when we allow ourselves warm-hearted patriotism, a plunge back into old loves and narrow views—I have just supplied an example. We have hours of national excitement, patriotic anguish, and every other old-fashioned flood of feeling. What runs its course in us within hours may take duller spirits a considerable time to finish with: half a year for some, half a lifetime for others, according to the speed and strength of their digestion and “change of material”. Indeed, I can imagine sluggish, hesitant races that, even in our fast-moving Europe, would need half a century to overcome such ancestral attacks of patriotism and attachment to the soil, and return to reason—that is, to “good Europeanism”. While considering this possibility, I happened to overhear two old patriots talking. Evidently both were hard of hearing, and therefore spoke all the louder. “HE possesses about as much philosophy, and knows about as much of it, as a peasant or a corps-student,” said one. “He is still innocent. But what does that matter today! This is the age of the masses: they prostrate themselves before everything massive. The same holds in politicis. They call a statesman ‘great’ if he builds them a new Tower of Babel, some monstrous empire and power. What do they care that we more cautious, conservative people still hold the old belief that only a great thought makes an action or undertaking great? Suppose a statesman forced his people henceforth to practise ‘high politics’, for which nature had poorly equipped and prepared them, so that they had to sacrifice their old, dependable virtues for the love of a new and doubtful mediocrity. Suppose he condemned his people to ‘practise politics’ altogether, when they had previously had better things to do and think about, and had never been able to shake off, deep in their souls, a sensible disgust at the restlessness, emptiness, and noisy quarrels of essentially political nations. Suppose he stirred his people's sleeping passions and greed, made their former reserve and love of standing apart into a disgrace, their exotic character and hidden persistence into an offence, disparaged their deepest inclinations, overturned their consciences, narrowed their minds, and made their tastes ‘national’—what! A statesman who did all this, for which his people would have to do penance throughout their future, if they had a future, would be GREAT, would he?” “Certainly!” the other old patriot answered fiercely. “Otherwise he COULD NOT have done it! Perhaps wanting such a thing was madness! But perhaps everything great began in just that kind of madness!” “Abuse of language!” his companion shouted back. “Strong! Strong! Strong and mad! NOT great!” The old men had plainly grown heated, shouting their “truths” into each other's faces. Happy and apart, I reflected on how soon someone stronger might master the strong, and on the compensation for one nation's intellectual shallowness: the deepening of another.

9.2.oldText: 242. Whether we call what now distinguishes the European “civilization”, “humanization”, or “progress”, or simply use the political formula of Europe's DEMOCRATIC movement without praise or blame, an immense PHYSIOLOGICAL PROCESS goes on behind the moral and political foreground these formulas indicate. Europeans increasingly grow alike; they increasingly detach themselves from the climatic and hereditary conditions in which unified races arise; they increasingly become independent of any particular environment that would impose the same demands on body and soul for centuries. In other words, an essentially SUPER-NATIONAL, nomadic human type slowly emerges, whose typical distinction, physiologically speaking, is the highest degree of skill and power in adaptation. Great setbacks may slow the TEMPO of this process of the EUROPEAN'S EVOLUTION, yet perhaps they will only increase its force and depth. The still-raging storm of “national feeling” belongs among these, as does the anarchism now appearing. This process will probably produce results its naive promoters and enthusiasts, the apostles of “modern ideas”, would least like to anticipate. The new conditions that, on average, level human beings into mediocrity—useful, industrious, clever herd people capable of many services—are also extraordinarily suited to producing exceptional people with the most dangerous and attractive qualities. Adaptability, daily testing changing circumstances and beginning new work with every generation, almost every decade, prevents the type from becoming POWERFUL. The collective impression of these future Europeans will probably be of numerous, talkative, weak-willed, very handy workers who NEED a master and commander as they need their daily bread. Thus Europe's democratization will tend to produce a type prepared for SLAVERY in the subtlest sense. Yet in individual, exceptional cases, the STRONG person will necessarily become stronger and richer than perhaps ever before, because of an unprejudiced education and an immense variety of practice, skills, and disguises. What I meant to say is that Europe's democratization also involuntarily prepares the breeding of TYRANTS—taking that word in every sense, including its most spiritual.

9.4.oldText: 244. Germans were once commonly singled out as “deep”. But now the most successful type of new Germanism hungers for quite different honours, perhaps finding everything deep deficient in “smartness”. It is almost timely and patriotic to wonder whether that old compliment deceived us: whether German depth is really something else and something worse, something we are, thank God, about to shed successfully. Let us therefore learn anew about German depth. All we need is a little vivisection of the German soul. Above all, that soul is multiple, varied in origin, piled up and layered rather than actually built: its ancestry accounts for this. A German bold enough to declare, “Two souls, alas, live in my breast”, would guess the truth badly—or, more precisely, fall far short of the true number of souls. The Germans are a people formed from an extraordinary mixing and mingling of races, perhaps even predominantly pre-Aryan; they are the “people of the centre” in every sense. Consequently they are more elusive, expansive, contradictory, unknown, incalculable, surprising, and even frightening to themselves than other peoples are. They evade DEFINITION, and that alone drives the French to despair. It IS characteristic of Germans that the question “What is German?” never dies among them. Kotzebue certainly knew his Germans well enough: “We are known”, they cried to him triumphantly—but Sand also thought he knew them. Jean Paul knew what he was doing when he expressed outrage at Fichte's dishonest but patriotic flatteries and exaggerations. Yet Goethe probably thought differently about the Germans from Jean Paul, even though he agreed with him about Fichte. What did Goethe really think about the Germans? On many matters around him he never spoke plainly, and throughout his life he knew how to maintain a shrewd silence, probably with good reason. Certainly neither the “Wars of Independence” nor the French Revolution made him look up with greater joy. The event that led him to RECONSTRUCT his “Faust”, and indeed the whole problem of “man”, was Napoleon's appearance. In some remarks Goethe condemns what Germans pride themselves on with impatient severity, as though speaking from abroad. He once defined the famous German cast of mind as “Indulgence towards its own and others' weaknesses”. Was he wrong? One characteristic of Germans is that people are seldom entirely wrong about them. The German soul contains passages, galleries, caves, hiding places, and dungeons. Its disorder has much of mystery's charm; the German knows the side roads to chaos well. Since everything loves its symbol, he loves clouds and everything obscure, developing, twilight-like, damp, and veiled. Whatever is uncertain, unfinished, shifting, and growing seems “deep” to him. The German himself does not EXIST: he is BECOMING, he is “developing himself”. Hence “development” is the specifically German discovery and success among philosophical formulas, a ruling idea that, together with German beer and music, works to Germanize all Europe. Foreigners are astonished and attracted by the riddles posed by the contradictory character at the German soul's base—riddles Hegel systematized and Richard Wagner finally set to music. “Good-natured and spiteful”: this combination, absurd for any other people, is unfortunately justified all too often in Germany. One need only live among Swabians for a while to know it! The German scholar's clumsiness and social unpleasantness fit alarmingly well with his physical tightrope-dancing and nimble daring, which all the gods have learned to fear. Anyone wanting the “German soul” demonstrated ad oculos need only look at German taste, arts, and manners: what boorish indifference to “taste”! How the noblest and commonest sit side by side! How disordered and rich this soul's whole constitution is! The German DRAGS his soul along; he drags everything he experiences. He digests events badly and never gets “finished” with them. German depth often amounts merely to difficult, hesitant “digestion”. Just as all chronic invalids and dyspeptics like convenience, the German loves “frankness” and “honesty”: being frank and honest is so CONVENIENT! This trustfulness, accommodation, and laying of cards on the table, this German HONESTY, is probably the most dangerous and successful disguise the German now knows. It is his particular Mephistophelean art; with it he can “still achieve much”! The German lets himself go and gazes out with faithful, blue, empty German eyes—and other countries immediately mistake him for his dressing gown! What I meant was this: whatever “German depth” may be, and perhaps among ourselves we take the liberty of laughing at it, we would do well to keep honouring its appearance and reputation. We should not trade our old reputation as a profound people too cheaply for Prussian “smartness” and Berlin wit and sand. It is wise for a people to pose, and LET itself be taken, as deep, clumsy, good-natured, honest, and foolish. Doing so might even be—profound! Finally, let us honour our name: we are not called the “TIUSCHE VOLK”, the deceptive people, for nothing....

9.5.oldText: 245. The “good old” age is gone; it sang itself to an end in Mozart. How fortunate WE are that his ROCOCO still speaks to us, that his “good company”, tender enthusiasm, childlike pleasure in Chinese things and their flourishes, courtesy of heart, longing for elegance, love, light steps and tears, and faith in the South can still appeal to SOMETHING REMAINING in us! Ah, one day that too will be over! But who doubts that understanding and taste for Beethoven will disappear even sooner! He was only the last echo of a break and transition in style, NOT, like Mozart, the final echo of a great European taste that had lasted for centuries. Beethoven stands between an old, mellow soul continually breaking down and a future soul, too young, always COMING. His music is covered by the twilight of eternal loss and eternal extravagant hope, the same light that bathed Europe when it dreamed with Rousseau, danced around the Revolution's Tree of Liberty, and finally almost fell down worshipping Napoleon. But how quickly THIS very feeling now fades, how hard it is today even to GRASP it. How strange to our ears is the language of Rousseau, Schiller, Shelley, and Byron, in whom TOGETHER the same European destiny could SPEAK that knew how to SING in Beethoven! All the German music that followed belongs to Romanticism, a movement historically shorter, more fleeting, and more superficial than that great interlude: Europe's transition from Rousseau to Napoleon and the rise of democracy. Weber—but what do WE care today about “Freischutz” and “Oberon”! Or Marschner's “Hans Heiling” and “Vampyre”! Or even Wagner's “Tannhauser”! This music is extinct, though not yet forgotten. Moreover, Romantic music as a whole was neither noble nor musical enough to hold its place anywhere except in the theatre and before the masses. From the beginning it was second-rate music, little esteemed by genuine musicians. Felix Mendelssohn was different, that serene master whose lighter, purer, happier soul won admiration quickly and was forgotten just as quickly: the beautiful EPISODE of German music. But Robert Schumann took things seriously and was taken seriously from the start; he was the last to establish a school. Don't we now feel satisfaction, relief, deliverance, that this very Romanticism of Schumann's has been overcome? Schumann fled into his soul's “Saxon Switzerland”, with a nature half like Werther and half like Jean Paul—certainly not like Beethoven! Certainly not like Byron! His MANFRED music is a mistake and misunderstanding amounting to an injustice. His taste was fundamentally PETTY: a dangerous inclination, doubly dangerous among Germans, towards quiet lyricism and intoxication with feelings. Always withdrawing, timidly retreating into seclusion, this noble weakling revelled only in anonymous joy and sorrow. A sort of girl and NOLI ME TANGERE from the beginning, Schumann was already merely a GERMAN event in music, no longer a European event as Beethoven had been and Mozart still more so. With Schumann, German music faced its greatest danger: LOSING ITS VOICE FOR EUROPE'S SOUL and sinking into a merely national concern.

9.11.oldText: 251. When a people suffers, and WANTS to suffer, from national nervous fever and political ambition, we must accept that clouds and disturbances will pass over its spirit—in short, little attacks of stupidity. Today's Germans, for example, alternate between anti-French folly, anti-Semitic folly, anti-Polish folly, Christian-romantic folly, Wagnerian folly, Teutonic folly, Prussian folly—just look at those poor historians, the Sybels and Treitschkes, with their tightly bandaged heads—and whatever other names these little darkenings of German spirit and conscience go by. Forgive me if I too failed to escape the disease completely during a brief, daring visit to heavily infected ground. Like everyone else, I began thinking about matters that did not concern me, the first symptom of political infection. About the Jews, for instance, listen to this. I have never yet met a German favourably disposed towards the Jews. However firmly all prudent, politically minded men reject actual anti-Semitism, perhaps their prudence and policy oppose only the feeling's dangerous excess, especially its distasteful, disgraceful expression, rather than the feeling itself. We must not deceive ourselves here. Germany has more than ENOUGH Jews; the German stomach, German blood, finds it difficult, and will long find it difficult, to deal with even this quantity of “Jew”, as Italians, Frenchmen, and Englishmen have done through stronger digestion. That is the unmistakable statement and language of a general instinct which must be heard and acted upon. “Let no more Jews enter! Close the doors, especially to the East, Austria included!” Thus commands the instinct of a people whose nature remains weak and uncertain, easily erased or extinguished by a stronger race. The Jews, however, are unquestionably the strongest, toughest, and purest race now living in Europe. They know how to succeed even under the worst conditions, indeed better than under favourable ones, through virtues of a sort people today would like to label vices. Above all, they possess a firm faith with no need to feel ashamed before “modern ideas”. WHEN they change at all, they change as the Russian Empire makes its conquests: like an empire with plenty of time, not born yesterday, following the principle “as slowly as possible”! A thinker concerned for Europe's future will count on the Jews, as on the Russians, in every view of that future, as the most reliable and probable factors in the great interplay and battle of forces. What Europe now calls a “nation” is really more RES FACTA than NATA, sometimes confusingly close to RES FICTA ET PICTA. In every case it is something developing, young, easily shifted, not yet a race, much less a race AERE PERENNUS like the Jews. Such “nations” should most carefully avoid hot-headed rivalry and hostility! Certainly the Jews COULD now gain ascendancy, indeed literal supremacy, over Europe if they wanted it, or were driven to it, as the anti-Semites seem to wish. It is equally certain that they are NOT working or planning towards that end. Instead, they now wish and desire, even somewhat insistently, to be taken into and absorbed by Europe. They long finally to settle somewhere, accepted and respected, ending nomadic life and the “wandering Jew”. We should certainly acknowledge this impulse and tendency and MEET IT HALFWAY; perhaps it signals a moderation of Jewish instincts. For that purpose it might be useful and fair to banish the anti-Semitic loudmouths from the country. We should make these approaches prudently and selectively, much as the English nobility does. Naturally, the stronger, more sharply defined types of new Germanism could enter relations with the Jews with least hesitation: for example, aristocratic officers from the Prussian border. It would be interesting in many ways to see whether a genius for money and patience, and especially some intellect and intellectuality, sadly lacking there, could be added and cultivated alongside the hereditary art of commanding and obeying, both of which already give that region a classic reputation. But here I should interrupt my festive speech and lively Teutonomania, for I have reached my SERIOUS SUBJECT: the “European problem” as I understand it, breeding a new ruling caste for Europe.

9.12.oldText: 252. The English are no philosophical race. Bacon represents an ATTACK on the philosophical spirit generally; Hobbes, Hume, and Locke represent a lowering and devaluation of the idea of a “philosopher” lasting more than a century. Kant rose up and raised himself AGAINST Hume; Schelling RIGHTLY said of Locke, “JE MEPRISE LOCKE”. In opposing the English mechanical reduction of the world to stupidity, Hegel and Schopenhauer agreed, as did Goethe. Those two hostile brother-geniuses of philosophy pushed in different directions towards opposite poles of German thought, wronging each other as only brothers can. What England lacks and has always lacked was well known to Carlyle, that half-actor and rhetorician, that absurd muddlehead. His passionate grimaces tried to conceal what he knew about himself: what Carlyle LACKED—real intellectual POWER, real DEPTH of understanding, in short, philosophy. Such an unphilosophical race characteristically clings to Christianity: it NEEDS Christianity's discipline to “moralize” and humanize it. The Englishman is gloomier, more sensual, headstrong, and brutal than the German; precisely as the baser of the two, he is also the more pious. His NEED for Christianity is that much GREATER. To sensitive nostrils, English Christianity itself still carries a distinctively English smell of spleen and alcoholic excess, against which it is, for good reasons, used as an antidote: the finer poison neutralizing the coarser. For coarse-mannered people, a finer poisoning really is progress, a step towards spirituality. Christian pantomime, prayer, and psalm-singing still disguise English coarseness and rustic primness most satisfactorily—or, more accurately, explain and express them differently. As for the herd of drunkards and rakes who once learned moral grunting under Methodism, and more recently as the “Salvation Army”, a fit of repentance may indeed be the relatively highest expression of “humanity” to which they can rise. We may reasonably concede that much. Yet even the most humane Englishman offends by his lack of music, figuratively and literally. His body's and soul's movements possess neither rhythm nor dance, not even a desire for rhythm, dance, “music”. Listen to his speech; watch the most beautiful Englishwoman WALKING—nowhere on earth are there lovelier doves and swans—and finally listen to them sing! But I ask too much...

9.13.oldText: 253. Some truths are best recognized by mediocre minds, being best suited to them; some truths have charm and seductive power only for mediocre spirits. We are driven to this probably unwelcome conclusion as respectable but mediocre Englishmen—Darwin, John Stuart Mill, and Herbert Spencer come to mind—begin to dominate the middle-class region of European taste. Indeed, who could doubt that it is useful for SUCH minds to prevail for a time? It would be mistaken to think highly developed, independently soaring minds especially suited to establishing and collecting many small, ordinary facts and drawing conclusions from them. As exceptions, they stand from the outset at something of a disadvantage towards those who are “the rules”. After all, they have more to do than perceive: they must BE something new, MEAN something new, REPRESENT new values! The gap between knowledge and ability may be larger, and more mysterious, than we suppose. The capable person on the grand scale, the creator, may have to be ignorant. Scientific discoveries like Darwin's, on the other hand, may benefit from a certain narrowness, dryness, and hardworking carefulness—in short, something English. Finally, remember that the English, with their profound mediocrity, once before brought about a general decline in European intelligence. What people call “modern ideas”, “the ideas of the eighteenth century”, or “French ideas”—against which the GERMAN spirit rose in profound disgust—is indisputably English in origin. The French merely aped and acted out these ideas; they were their best soldiers and, alas! their first and deepest VICTIMS. Through the devilish Anglomania of “modern ideas”, the AME FRANCAIS has finally grown so thin and wasted that we now recall its sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, its deep, passionate strength and outstanding inventiveness, almost in disbelief. Yet we must firmly uphold this historically just verdict against present prejudices and appearances: European NOBLESSE, in feeling, taste, and manners, in every elevated meaning of the word, is FRANCE'S work and invention. European ignobility, the plebeianism of modern ideas, is ENGLAND'S work and invention.

9.14.oldText: 254. Even today France remains the home of Europe's most intellectual, refined culture, its advanced school of taste. But one must know how to find this “France of taste”. Those who belong to it stay well hidden. Perhaps only a few embody and sustain it, and perhaps they do not stand on very strong legs: some are fatalists, hypochondriacs, invalids; others overindulged, overrefined people whose AMBITION is to conceal themselves. All share one trait: they close their ears to the democratic BOURGEOIS's delirious folly and noisy outpourings. For a stupefied, brutalized France now sprawls in the foreground. At Victor Hugo's funeral it recently celebrated a genuine orgy of bad taste and self-admiration. These hidden people share something else: a desire to resist intellectual Germanization—and an even greater inability to do so! In this intellectual France, also a pessimistic France, Schopenhauer has perhaps become more at home and more native than he ever was in Germany. Not to mention Heinrich Heine, long since reincarnated in Paris's more refined and demanding lyric poets; or Hegel, who now exercises an almost tyrannical influence in the form of Taine, the FOREMOST living historian. As for Richard Wagner, the more French music learns to adapt to the actual needs of the AME MODERNE, the more it will “Wagnerite”. We can safely predict that: it is already happening enough! Nevertheless, despite every willing or unwilling Germanization and vulgarization of taste, the French can still proudly claim three things as their inheritance and possession, indelible signs of their old intellectual superiority in Europe. FIRST, their capacity for artistic feeling and devotion to “form”, for which L'ART POUR L'ART and many other expressions were invented. France has possessed this capacity for three centuries. Its respect for the “small number” has repeatedly made possible a kind of chamber music of literature, sought in vain elsewhere in Europe. SECOND, the French can claim superiority through their old, many-sided MORALISTIC culture. Thanks to it, even minor newspaper ROMANCIERS and random BOULEVARDIERS DE PARIS generally display a psychological sensitivity and curiosity of which Germany, for example, has no conception, let alone the thing itself! Germans lack a couple of centuries of the necessary moralistic work which, as I said, France has willingly undertaken. Calling Germans “naive” on that account praises a deficiency. Set against German inexperience and innocence IN VOLUPTATE PSYCHOLOGICA, which is not unconnected with the tedium of German company, stands Henri Beyle. He is the most successful expression of genuine French curiosity and inventiveness in this realm of delicate thrills: that remarkable man who anticipated and ran ahead, traversing HIS Europe with a Napoleonic TEMPO, surveying and discovering, in effect, several centuries of the European soul. It took two generations to CATCH UP with him in one way or another, to divine long afterwards some of the riddles that troubled and enchanted this strange Epicurean and questioner, France's last great psychologist. There is a THIRD claim to superiority: French character successfully combines North and South halfway between them. This makes the French understand many things and imposes other things on them that an Englishman can never comprehend. Their temperament turns alternately towards and away from the South, with Provencal and Ligurian blood occasionally bubbling over. It protects them from the dreadful northern grey-on-grey, from sunless spectral abstractions and impoverished blood, that GERMAN sickness of taste. Its current prevalence has prompted the firm prescription of blood and iron, meaning “high politics”, according to a dangerous healing art that makes me wait and wait, but not yet hope. France also retains an instinctive understanding and ready welcome for rarer, seldom-satisfied people too comprehensive to find contentment in any patriotism. They know how to love the South in the North and the North in the South: born Midlanders, “good Europeans”. BIZET made music for them, this latest genius who saw a new beauty and seduction, who discovered a piece of the SOUTH IN MUSIC.

9.16.oldText: 256. The nationalistic craze has caused, and still causes, a sickly estrangement among Europe's nations. Shortsighted, hasty politicians now hold power with its help, never suspecting how necessarily temporary their policy of disintegration must be. Because of all this, and much else that cannot presently be mentioned, people now overlook the clearest signs that EUROPE WANTS TO BE ONE, or wilfully misinterpret them. Among this century's deeper, broader-minded men, the true general direction of their souls' mysterious work was to prepare that new SYNTHESIS and tentatively anticipate the future European. Only in their poses, or their weaker moments, perhaps in old age, did they belong to the “fatherlands”. When they became “patriots”, they were merely resting from themselves. I mean such men as Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heinrich Heine, and Schopenhauer. Do not take it amiss if I include Richard Wagner. We must not let his own misunderstandings deceive us about him—geniuses like him seldom have the right to understand themselves—still less the unseemly noise of present French resistance and opposition to him. The fact remains that Richard Wagner and the LATER FRENCH ROMANTICISM of the forties are intimately, closely related. Their kinship is fundamental, in every height and depth of their demands. In their varied, tumultuous art, it is Europe, ONE Europe, whose soul urgently and longingly presses outward and upward—where? Into a new light? Towards a new sun? But who would try to state precisely what all these masters of new languages could not express distinctly? Certainly the same storm and stress tormented them; these last great seekers SOUGHT in the same way! All were steeped in literature up to their eyes and ears, the first artists of universal literary culture. Most were themselves writers and poets, mediators and mixers of arts and senses: Wagner as musician belongs among painters, as poet among musicians, as artist generally among actors. All were fanatics for EXPRESSION “at any cost”—I especially name Delacroix, Wagner's closest relative. All made great discoveries in the sublime, and also in the disgusting and terrifying; greater still were their discoveries in effect, display, and the art of the show-shop. Their talent exceeded even their genius; they were VIRTUOSI through and through, with mysterious access to everything that seduces, attracts, compels, and overturns. Born enemies of logic and the straight line, they craved the strange, exotic, monstrous, crooked, and contradictory. As people, they were Tantaluses of the will, plebeian upstarts who knew themselves incapable of a noble TEMPO or LENTO in life and action—think of Balzac, for instance. Unrestrained workers, they nearly destroyed themselves through work; rebels against laws and conventions of conduct, ambitious and insatiable, without balance or enjoyment. All finally shattered and sank before the Christian cross, with reason and justice: which of them was deep and original enough for an ANTI-CHRISTIAN philosophy? Taken together, they were a boldly daring, magnificently overbearing class of higher men, soaring and dragging others upward, who first had to teach their century—and it was the century of the MASSES—the concept “higher man”... Let Richard Wagner's German friends discuss whether anything in his art is purely German, or whether its distinction lies precisely in sources and impulses BEYOND GERMANY. In this connection, do not underestimate how indispensable Paris was to the development of his type. At the decisive moment, the force of his instincts made him long to visit it; the entire style of his activity, of his self-appointed apostolate, could perfect itself only in sight of the French socialist original. A subtler comparison may find, to the credit of Wagner's German nature, that he acted in everything with greater strength, daring, severity, and elevation than a nineteenth-century Frenchman could have done, because we Germans are still closer to barbarism than the French. Perhaps Wagner's most remarkable creation is inaccessible, incomprehensible, and inimitable to the entire late Latin race, not just now but forever: Siegfried, that VERY FREE man, probably far too free, hard, cheerful, healthy, and ANTI-CATHOLIC for the taste of old, mellow civilizations. This anti-Latin Siegfried may even have sinned against Romanticism. Well, Wagner amply atoned for that sin in his sad old age. Anticipating a taste that has since entered politics, he began, with his characteristic religious fervour, at least to preach THE ROAD TO ROME, if not to walk it. To prevent misunderstanding of those last words, I call on a few forceful rhymes. They will reveal even to less sensitive ears what I mean, what I mean AGAINST the “last Wagner” and his Parsifal music: Is this our way? From German hearts, this tortured wailing? From German flesh, this self-assailing? These priestly hands spread wide in prayer, This incense rising through the air? This faltering, falling, stumbling motion, This wavering ding-dong of devotion? These sly looks at nuns, these Ave bells ringing, This utterly false, ecstatic heavenward springing? Is this our way? Think hard! You still await admission: What you hear is ROME—ROME'S FAITH BY INTUITION!

10.0.oldText: 257. Every elevation of the type "man" has so far been the work of an aristocratic society — and so it will always be. Such a society believes in a long ladder of rank and worth among human beings, and it requires slavery in some form. Without the pathos of distance — the distance that grows from an embodied difference of classes, from the ruling caste's habit of looking out and down upon its subordinates and instruments, from its constant practice of obeying and commanding, of holding down and holding apart — that other, more mysterious pathos could never have arisen: the longing for an ever-greater widening of distance within the soul itself, the formation of ever higher, rarer, further, more extended, more comprehensive states — in short, the elevation of the type "man," the continued self-overcoming of man, to use a moral formula in a supermoral sense. One must not indulge any humanitarian illusions about the origin of an aristocratic society — that is, the precondition for the elevation of the type "man." The truth is hard. Let us acknowledge without prejudice how every higher civilization has hitherto originated! Men with a still natural nature, barbarians in every terrible sense of the word, men of prey, still possessed of unbroken strength of will and lust for power, flung themselves upon weaker, more moral, more peaceful races (perhaps trading or cattle-rearing communities), or upon old mellow civilizations in which the final vital force was flickering out in brilliant fireworks of wit and depravity. At the start, the noble caste was always the barbarian caste: their superiority lay not first of all in their physical but in their psychical power — they were more complete men (which at every point also means: more complete beasts).

10.2.oldText: 259. To refrain mutually from injury, violence, and exploitation, and to put one's will on a par with that of others — this can, in a certain rough sense, make for good conduct among individuals, provided the necessary conditions are present (that the individuals are actually similar in force and worth, and co-related within one organization). The moment one wishes to take this principle more generally, and possibly even as the fundamental principle of society, it at once reveals what it really is: a will to the denial of life, a principle of dissolution and decay. One must think here profoundly, to the very roots, and resist all sentimental weakness. Life itself is essentially appropriation, injury, conquest of the strange and weak, suppression, severity, the imposition of one's own forms, incorporation — at the very least and mildest: exploitation. But why should one forever use precisely these words, on which disparaging intent has long been stamped? Even that organization within which, as was previously supposed, individuals treat each other as equal — as happens in every healthy aristocracy — must itself, if it is a living and not a dying organization, do toward other bodies all that its members refrain from doing to one another. It will have to be an embodied will to power; it will seek to grow, to gain ground, to attract to itself and win ascendancy — not out of any morality or immorality, but because it lives, and because life is precisely will to power. On no point is the ordinary consciousness of Europeans more unwilling to be corrected than on this. People rave everywhere, even under the banner of science, about future conditions of society in which "the exploiting character" will be absent. To my ears that sounds as if they promised to invent a mode of life that dispensed with all organic functions. Exploitation does not belong to a depraved or primitive society; it belongs to the nature of the living being as a primary organic function. It is a consequence of the intrinsic will to power, which is precisely the will to life. As a theory this may be a novelty — as a reality it is the fundamental fact of all history. Let us be at least this honest with ourselves!

10.3.oldText: 260. On a journey through the many finer and coarser moralities that have prevailed or still prevail on earth, I found certain traits recurring together and linked with one another, until at last two primary types emerged and a fundamental distinction came to light. There is master-morality and slave-morality. I should add at once that in all higher and mixed civilizations there are also attempts at reconciling the two — more often still their confusion and mutual misunderstanding, and sometimes their close juxtaposition, even within the same man, within one soul. The distinctions of moral values have originated either in a ruling caste, pleasantly conscious of being different from those it ruled, or among the ruled — the slaves and dependents of every kind. In the first case, when it is the rulers who determine the concept "good," it is the exalted, proud states of soul that are felt to be what distinguishes and determines rank. The noble type of man separates from himself those in whom the opposite of such states shows itself; he despises them. It should be noted that in this first kind of morality the opposition "good" and "bad" means practically the same as "noble" and "despicable." The opposition "good" and "evil" has a different origin. The cowardly, the timid, the petty, those who think only of narrow utility are despised; so too the distrustful with their constrained glances, the self-abasing, the dog-like men who let themselves be mistreated, the mendicant flatterers, and above all the liars. It is a fundamental belief of all aristocrats that the common people are untruthful. "We truthful ones" — so the nobility called itself in ancient Greece. It is obvious that moral designations were first applied to men and only derivatively, at a later period, to actions. Historians of morals therefore make a gross mistake when they start with questions like "Why have sympathetic actions been praised?" The noble type of man feels himself to be the determiner of values. He does not require approval; he passes judgment: "What harms me is harmful in itself." He knows that it is he alone who confers honor on things; he is a creator of values. He honors whatever he recognizes in himself: such morality is self-glorification. In the foreground is the feeling of fullness, of power that seeks to overflow, the happiness of high tension, the consciousness of a wealth that would gladly give and bestow. The noble man also helps the unfortunate, but not — or scarcely — out of pity; rather from an impulse generated by the superabundance of power. The noble man honors in himself the powerful one, the man who has power over himself, who knows how to speak and how to keep silent, who takes pleasure in subjecting himself to severity and hardness, and who has reverence for all that is severe and hard. "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast," an old Scandinavian saga says — rightly expressed from the soul of a proud Viking. Such a man is even proud of not being made for sympathy, and so the saga hero adds a warning: "He who has not a hard heart when young will never have one." The noble and brave who think in this way are the furthest removed from a morality that sees the characteristic of the moral precisely in sympathy, in acting for others, in désintéressement. Faith in oneself, pride in oneself, a fundamental enmity and irony toward "selflessness" — these belong as surely to noble morality as do a careless scorn and caution in the presence of sympathy and the "warm heart." It is the powerful who know how to honor; it is their art, their realm of invention. Profound reverence for age and tradition — all law rests on this double reverence — the belief and prejudice in favor of ancestors and against newcomers, is typical of the morality of the powerful. If, conversely, men of "modern ideas" believe almost instinctively in "progress" and "the future," and show less and less respect for age, the ignoble origin of these "ideas" has complacently betrayed itself. A morality of the ruling class is, however, most foreign and irritating to present-day taste in the sternness of its principle that one has duties only to one's equals; that toward beings of lower rank, toward all that is foreign, one may act as one pleases, or "as the heart desires," and in any case "beyond good and evil" — here sympathy and similar sentiments can find their place. The ability and duty to exercise prolonged gratitude and prolonged revenge — both only within the circle of equals — artfulness in retaliation, raffinement of the idea of friendship, a certain need for enemies (as outlets for the emotions of envy, quarrelsomeness, arrogance — in order, in fact, to be a good friend): all these are typical features of noble morality. As noted, it is not the morality of "modern ideas," and is therefore hard to realize today, and also hard to unearth and uncover. It is otherwise with the second type of morality, slave-morality. Suppose that the abused, the oppressed, the suffering, the unfree, the weary, and those uncertain of themselves moralize — what will be the common element in their moral estimates? A pessimistic suspicion about the entire human situation will probably find expression, perhaps a condemnation of man together with his situation. The slave has an unfavorable eye for the virtues of the powerful; he has a skepticism and distrust, a refinement of distrust for everything "good" that is honored there — he would like to persuade himself that even their happiness is not genuine. On the other hand, those qualities that serve to ease the existence of sufferers are brought forward and bathed in light: here sympathy, the kind and helping hand, the warm heart, patience, diligence, humility, and friendliness come to honor, for here these are the most useful qualities and almost the only means of bearing the burden of existence. Slave-morality is essentially a morality of utility. Here is the origin of the famous opposition "good" and "evil": power and dangerousness are assumed to reside in the evil — a certain dreadfulness, subtlety, and strength that do not allow themselves to be despised. According to slave-morality, then, the "evil" man arouses fear; according to master-morality, it is precisely the "good" man who arouses and wishes to arouse fear, while the "bad" man is thought of as the despicable being. The contrast reaches its peak when, in consistency with slave-morality, a shade of disparagement — it may be slight and well-meaning — attaches itself at last to the "good" man of this morality. On the servile mode of thought, the good man must in any case be the safe man: good-natured, easily deceived, perhaps a little stupid, un bonhomme. Wherever slave-morality gains ascendancy, language shows a tendency to approximate the meanings of the words "good" and "stupid." One last fundamental difference: the desire for freedom, the instinct for happiness, and the refinements of the feeling of liberty belong as necessarily to slave-morality as artifice and enthusiasm in reverence and devotion are the regular symptoms of an aristocratic mode of thinking and valuing. From this it is easy to see why love as a passion — our European speciality — must be of noble origin; its invention, as is well known, is owed to the Provençal knight-poets, those brilliant, ingenious men of the gai saber, to whom Europe owes so much, and almost owes itself.

10.5.oldText: 262. A species originates, and a type becomes established and strong, through the long struggle with essentially constant unfavorable conditions. On the other hand, breeders know by experience that species receiving superabundant nourishment, and in general a surplus of protection and care, immediately tend to develop variations strongly marked, and become fertile in prodigies and monstrosities (including monstrous vices). Now look at an aristocratic commonwealth — say, an ancient Greek polis or Venice — as a voluntary or involuntary arrangement for the rearing of human beings. There are men side by side, thrown on their own resources, who want to make their kind prevail, chiefly because they must prevail — or else face the terrible danger of extermination. The favor, the superabundance, the protection under which variations are fostered are lacking; the species needs itself as species, as something that, precisely through its hardness, its uniformity, and simplicity of structure, can prevail and make itself permanent in constant struggle with neighbors or with rebellious or rebellion-threatening vassals. The most varied experience teaches it what qualities have allowed it to exist despite all gods and men and have so far made it victorious: these qualities it calls virtues, and these alone it cultivates to maturity. It does so with severity — indeed it desires severity. Every aristocratic morality is intolerant in the education of youth, in the control of women, in marriage customs, in the relations of old and young, in penal laws (which have an eye only for the degenerate); it even counts intolerance among the virtues, under the name of "justice." A type with few but strongly marked features, a species of severe, warlike, shrewdly silent, reserved, and reticent men (who, precisely as such, have the most delicate sensibility for the charm and nuances of society), is thus established, unaffected by the vicissitudes of generations. The constant struggle with uniformly unfavorable conditions is, as noted, the cause of a type becoming stable and hard. Finally, however, a happy state comes: the enormous tension relaxes; perhaps there are no more enemies among neighboring peoples, and the means of life — even of the enjoyment of life — are present in superabundance. At one stroke the bond and constraint of the old discipline is severed: it is no longer felt necessary, no longer a condition of existence — if it is to continue, it can only do so as a form of luxury, as an archaizing taste. Variations, whether they be deviations (into the higher, finer, and rarer) or deteriorations and monstrosities, now appear suddenly on the scene in the greatest exuberance and splendor. The individual dares to be individual and to detach himself. At this turning point of history there appear, side by side and often mixed and entangled together, a magnificent, virgin-forest-like upward growth and upward striving, a kind of tropical tempo in the rivalry of growth, and an extraordinary decay and self-destruction, owing to the savagely opposing and seemingly exploding egoisms that strive against one another "for sun and light" and can no longer assign themselves any limit, restraint, or forbearance through the existing morality. It was this morality itself that piled up the strength so enormously, that bent the bow in so threatening a manner; it is now "out of date," it is getting "out of date." The dangerous and disquieting point has been reached when the greater, more manifold, more comprehensive life is lived beyond the old morality. The "individual" stands out and is obliged to have recourse to his own lawgiving, his own arts and artifices, for self-preservation, self-elevation, and self-deliverance. Nothing but new "Whys," nothing but new "Hows," no common formulas any longer; misunderstanding and disregard leagued together; decay, deterioration, and the loftiest desires frightfully entangled; the genius of the race overflowing from all the cornucopias of good and bad; a portentous simultaneity of spring and autumn, full of new charms and mysteries peculiar to the fresh, still inexhausted, still unwearied corruption. Danger is again present — the mother of morality — great danger, this time shifted into the individual, into neighbor and friend, into the street, into one's own child, into one's own heart, into all the most personal and secret recesses of desire and will. What will the moral philosophers of this time have to preach? They discover, these sharp observers and loafers, that the end is quickly approaching, that everything around them decays and produces decay, that nothing will last until the day after tomorrow — except one species of man, the incurably mediocre. The mediocre alone have a prospect of continuing and propagating themselves; they will be the men of the future, the sole survivors. "Be like them! Become mediocre!" is now the only morality that still has significance, that still gets a hearing. But it is difficult to preach this morality of mediocrity! It can never admit what it is and what it wants! It has to speak of moderation and dignity and duty and brotherly love — it will have trouble concealing its irony!

10.7.oldText: 264. It cannot be effaced from a man's soul what his ancestors most preferably and constantly did: whether they were perhaps diligent economizers attached to a desk and a cash-box, modest and citizen-like in their desires and in their virtues; or whether they were accustomed to commanding from morning till night, fond of rough pleasures and probably of rougher duties and responsibilities; or whether, finally, at some time they sacrificed old privileges of birth and possession in order to live wholly for their faith — for their "God" — as men of an inexorable and sensitive conscience that blushes at every compromise. It is quite impossible for a man not to have the qualities and predilections of his parents and ancestors in his constitution, whatever appearances may suggest to the contrary. This is the problem of race. Given that one knows something of the parents, one may draw a conclusion about the child: any kind of offensive incontinence, any kind of sordid envy, any kind of clumsy self-vaunting — the three things which together have constituted the genuine plebeian type in all times — must pass to the child as surely as bad blood; and with the help of the best education and culture one will only succeed in deceiving about such heredity. And what else does education and culture try to do nowadays! In our very democratic — or rather, very plebeian — age, "education" and "culture" must be essentially the art of deceiving: deceiving about origin, about the inherited plebeianism in body and soul. An educator who today preached truthfulness above everything else and constantly called out to his pupils, "Be true! Be natural! Show yourselves as you are!" — even such a virtuous and sincere ass would soon learn to resort to Horace's furca — naturam expellere — and with what results? Plebeianism usque recurret. [Footnote: Horace's "Epistles," I. x. 24.]

10.8.oldText: 265. At the risk of displeasing innocent ears, I submit that egoism belongs to the essence of a noble soul — I mean the unalterable belief that to a being such as "we," other beings must naturally be in subjection and must sacrifice themselves. The noble soul accepts the fact of his egoism without question, and also without any feeling of harshness, constraint, or arbitrariness, but rather as something that may have its basis in the primary law of things. If he sought a name for it, he would say: "It is justice itself." He acknowledges under certain circumstances, though they made him hesitate at first, that there are other equally privileged ones. As soon as he has settled this question of rank, he moves among these equals with the same assurance of modesty and delicate respect as he enjoys in dealing with himself — in accordance with an innate heavenly mechanism that all the stars understand. This artfulness and self-limitation in intercourse with his equals is another instance of his egoism: every star is a similar egoist. He honors himself in them, and in the rights he concedes to them; he has no doubt that the exchange of honors and rights, as the essence of all intercourse, belongs also to the natural condition of things. The noble soul gives as he takes, prompted by the passionate and sensitive instinct of requital that is at the root of his nature. The notion of "favor," inter pares, has neither significance nor good repute; there may be a sublime way of letting gifts, as it were, light upon one from above, and of drinking them thirstily like dew-drops, but the noble soul has no aptitude for those arts and displays. His egoism prevents it: in general he looks "aloft" unwillingly — he looks either forward, horizontally and deliberately, or downward: he knows that he is on a height.

10.12.oldText: 269. The more a psychologist — a born, an unavoidable psychologist and soul-diviner — turns his attention to the more select cases and individuals, the greater is his danger of being suffocated by sympathy. He needs sternness and cheerfulness more than any other man. For the corruption and ruination of higher men, of the more unusually constituted souls, is in fact the rule: it is dreadful to have such a rule always before one's eyes. The manifold torment of the psychologist who has discovered this ruination, who discovers it once and then discovers it almost repeatedly throughout all history — this universal inner "desperateness" of higher men, this eternal "too late!" in every sense — may perhaps one day cause him to turn with bitterness against his own lot and to attempt self-destruction: to "go to ruin" himself. In almost every psychologist one may perceive a telltale inclination for delightful intercourse with commonplace and well-ordered men; the fact is thereby disclosed that he always requires healing, that he needs a sort of flight and forgetfulness, away from what his insight and incisiveness — his "business" — has laid upon his conscience. The fear of his memory is peculiar to him. He is easily silenced by the judgment of others; he hears with unmoved countenance how people honor, admire, love, and glorify where he has perceived, or he even conceals his silence by expressly assenting to some plausible opinion. Perhaps the paradox of his situation becomes so dreadful that precisely where he has learned great sympathy together with great contempt, the multitude, the educated, and the visionaries have on their part learned great reverence — reverence for "great men" and marvelous animals for whose sake one blesses and honors the fatherland, the earth, the dignity of mankind, and oneself, to whom one points the young, and in view of whom one educates them. And who knows but in all great instances hitherto the same happened: that the multitude worshipped a god, and that the "god" was only a poor sacrificial animal! Success has always been the greatest liar — and the "work" itself is a success. The great statesman, the conqueror, the discoverer, are disguised in their creations until they are unrecognizable. The "work" of the artist or philosopher invents only the man who is credited with having created it; the "great men," as they are reverenced, are poor little fictions composed afterward. In the world of historical values, spurious coinage prevails. Those great poets — Byron, Musset, Poe, Leopardi, Kleist, Gogol (I do not venture to mention much greater names, but I have them in mind) — as they now appear, and perhaps had to be: men of the moment, enthusiastic, sensuous, and childish, light-minded and impulsive in their trust and distrust; with souls in which some flaw usually has to be concealed; often taking revenge with their works for an inner defilement, often seeking forgetfulness in their soaring from a too-true memory, often lost in the mud and almost in love with it, until they become like the will-o'-the-wisps around the swamps and pretend to be stars — the people then call them idealists — often struggling with protracted disgust, with an ever-reappearing phantom of disbelief that makes them cold and obliges them to languish for gloria and devour "faith as it is" from the hands of intoxicated adulators: what a torment these great artists and so-called higher men are to one who has once found them out! It is thus conceivable that it is just from woman — who is clairvoyant in the world of suffering, and also unfortunately eager to help and save far beyond her powers — that they have so readily learned those outbreaks of boundless devoted sympathy, which the multitude, especially the reverent multitude, do not understand, and which they overwhelm with prying and self-gratifying interpretations. This sympathizing invariably deceives itself as to its power; woman would like to believe that love can do everything — it is the superstition peculiar to her. Alas, he who knows the heart finds out how poor, helpless, pretentious, and blundering even the best and deepest love is — that it rather destroys than saves! It is possible that under the holy fable and travesty of the life of Jesus there is hidden one of the most painful cases of the martyrdom of knowledge about love: the martyrdom of the most innocent and most craving heart, one that never had enough of any human love, that demanded love, that demanded inexorably and frantically to be loved and nothing else, with terrible outbursts against those who refused him their love; the story of a poor soul insatiated and insatiable in love, that had to invent hell to send there those who would not love him — and that at last, enlightened about human love, had to invent a God who is entire love, entire capacity for love — who takes pity on human love, because it is so paltry, so ignorant! He who has such sentiments, he who has such knowledge about love — seeks death! But why dwell on such painful matters? Unless, of course, one is obliged to.

10.13.oldText: 270. The intellectual haughtiness and loathing of every man who has suffered deeply — it almost determines the order of rank how deeply men can suffer — the chilling certainty, with which he is thoroughly imbued and colored, that by virtue of his suffering he knows more than the shrewdest and wisest can ever know, that he has been familiar with, and "at home" in, many distant, dreadful worlds of which "you know nothing"! — this silent intellectual haughtiness of the sufferer, this pride of the elect of knowledge, of the "initiated," of the almost sacrificed, finds all forms of disguise necessary to protect itself from contact with officious and sympathizing hands, and in general from all that is not its equal in suffering. Profound suffering makes noble: it separates. One of the most refined forms of disguise is Epicureanism, along with a certain ostentatious boldness of taste that takes suffering lightly and puts itself on the defensive against all that is sorrowful and profound. They are "gay men" who make use of gaiety because they are misunderstood on account of it — they wish to be misunderstood. There are "scientific minds" who make use of science because it gives a gay appearance, and because scientificness leads to the conclusion that a person is superficial — they wish to mislead to a false conclusion. There are free insolent minds who would like to conceal and deny that they are broken, proud, incurable hearts (the cynicism of Hamlet — the case of Galiani); and occasionally folly itself is the mask of an unfortunate, over-assured knowledge. From all this it follows that it is the part of a more refined humanity to have reverence "for the mask," and not to make use of psychology and curiosity in the wrong place.

The highest instinct for purity places him who is possessed of it in the most extraordinary and dangerous isolation, as a saint: for it is just holiness — the highest spiritualization of this instinct. 10.16.oldText: 273. A man who strives after great things looks upon everyone he meets on his way either as a means of advance, or as a delay and hindrance, or as a temporary resting place. His peculiar lofty bounty to his fellow-men is only possible when he has attained his elevation and dominates. Impatience, and the consciousness of being always condemned to comedy up to that time — for even strife is a comedy, and conceals the end, as every means does — spoil all intercourse for him; this kind of man is acquainted with solitude, and with what is most poisonous in it.

10.20.oldText: 277. It is too bad! Always the old story! When a man has finished building his house, he finds that he has learnt unawares something he absolutely ought to have known before he began to build. The eternal, fatal "Too late!" The melancholia of everything completed! 278. — Wanderer, who art thou? I see thee follow thy path without scorn, without love, with unfathomable eyes, wet and sad as a plummet which has returned to the light insatiated out of every depth — what did it seek down there? — with a bosom that never sighs, with lips that conceal their loathing, with a hand that grasps only slowly: who art thou? what hast thou done? Rest thee here: this place offers hospitality to everyone — refresh thyself! And whoever thou art, what is it that now pleases thee? What will serve to refresh thee? Only name it, whatever I have I offer thee! "To refresh me? To refresh me? Oh, thou prying one, what sayest thou! But give me, I pray thee — " What? what? Speak out! "Another mask! A second mask!"

10.22.oldText: 280. "Bad! Bad! What? Does he not — go back?" Yes! But you misunderstand him when you complain of it. He goes back like every one who is about to make a great spring. 281. — "Will people believe it of me? But I insist that they believe it of me: I have always thought very unsatisfactorily about myself, only in very rare cases, only compulsorily, always without delight in 'the subject,' ready to digress from 'myself,' and always without faith in the result, owing to an unconquerable distrust of the possibility of self-knowledge — a distrust that has led me so far as to feel a contradictio in adjecto even in the idea of 'direct knowledge' which theorists allow themselves. This matter of fact is almost the most certain thing I know about myself. There must be some sort of repugnance in me to believing anything definite about myself. Is there perhaps some enigma in this? Probably; but fortunately nothing for my own teeth. Perhaps it betrays the species to which I belong? — but not to myself, as is sufficiently agreeable to me." 282. — "But what has happened to you?" — "I do not know," he said, hesitantly; "perhaps the Harpies have flown over my table." — It sometimes happens nowadays that a gentle, sober, retiring man suddenly becomes mad, breaks the plates, upsets the table, shrieks, raves, and shocks everybody — and at last withdraws, ashamed and raging at himself — whither? for what purpose? To starve apart? To suffocate with his memories? To him who has the desires of a lofty and dainty soul, and only seldom finds his table laid and his food prepared, the danger will always be great — nowadays extraordinarily so. Thrown into the midst of a noisy and plebeian age, from which he does not like to eat out of the same dish, he may readily perish of hunger and thirst — or, should he nevertheless finally "fall to," he may perish of sudden nausea. We have probably all sat at tables to which we did not belong; and precisely the most spiritual among us, who are hardest to nourish, know the dangerous dyspepsia that arises from a sudden insight and disillusionment about our food and our messmates — the after-dinner nausea.

10.24.oldText: 284. To live in a vast and proud tranquility; always beyond… To have, or not to have, one's emotions, one's For and Against, according to choice; to lower oneself to them for hours; to seat oneself on them as upon horses, and often as upon asses — for one must know how to make use of their stupidity as well as of their fire. To conserve one's three hundred foregrounds; also one's black spectacles: for there are circumstances when nobody must look into our eyes, still less into our "motives." And to choose for company that roguish and cheerful vice, politeness. And to remain master of one's four virtues: courage, insight, sympathy, and solitude. For solitude is a virtue with us, as a sublime bent and bias toward purity, which divines that in the contact of man and man — "in society" — it must be unavoidably impure. All society somehow, somewhere, or sometime makes one "commonplace."

10.33.oldText: 293. A man who says: "I like that, I take it for my own, and mean to guard and protect it from every one"; a man who can conduct a case, carry out a resolution, remain true to an opinion, keep hold of a woman, punish and overthrow insolence; a man who has his indignation and his sword, and to whom the weak, the suffering, the oppressed — and even the animals — willingly submit and naturally belong; in short, a man who is a master by nature — when such a man has sympathy, well! That sympathy has value! But of what account is the sympathy of those who suffer! Or of those who even preach sympathy! There is nowadays, throughout almost the whole of Europe, a sickly irritability and sensitiveness toward pain, and also a repulsive unrestrainedness in complaining, an effeminization that, with the aid of religion and philosophical nonsense, seeks to dress itself up as something superior — there is a regular cult of suffering. The unmanliness of what is called "sympathy" by such groups of visionaries is always, I believe, the first thing that strikes the eye. One must resolutely and radically taboo this latest form of bad taste; and finally I wish people to put the good amulet, gai saber ("gay science," in ordinary language), on heart and neck, as a protection against it.

10.34.oldText: 294. The Olympian vice. — Despite the philosopher who, as a genuine Englishman, tried to bring laughter into bad repute in all thinking minds — "Laughing is a bad infirmity of human nature, which every thinking mind will strive to overcome" (Hobbes) — I would even allow myself to rank philosophers according to the quality of their laughing — up to those who are capable of golden laughter. And supposing that gods also philosophize, which I am strongly inclined to believe, owing to many reasons — I have no doubt that they also know how to laugh thereby in an overman-like and new fashion — and at the expense of all serious things! Gods are fond of ridicule: it seems that they cannot refrain from laughter even in holy matters.

10.35.oldText: 295. The genius of the heart, as that great mysterious one possesses it — the tempter-god and born rat-catcher of consciences, whose voice can descend into the nether-world of every soul; who neither speaks a word nor casts a glance in which there is not some motive or touch of allurement; to whose perfection it pertains that he knows how to appear — not as he is, but in a guise that acts as an additional constraint on his followers to press ever closer to him, to follow him more cordially and thoroughly; the genius of the heart, which imposes silence and attention on everything loud and self-conceited, which smooths rough souls and makes them taste a new longing — to lie placid as a mirror, that the deep heavens may be reflected in them; the genius of the heart, which teaches the clumsy and too-hasty hand to hesitate, and to grasp more delicately; which scents the hidden and forgotten treasure, the drop of goodness and sweet spirituality under thick dark ice, and is a divining-rod for every grain of gold long buried and imprisoned in mud and sand; the genius of the heart, from contact with which everyone goes away richer — not favored or surprised, not as though gratified and oppressed by the good things of others, but richer in himself, newer than before, broken up, blown upon, and sounded by a thawing wind; more uncertain perhaps, more delicate, more fragile, more bruised, but full of hopes which as yet lack names, full of a new will and current, full of a new ill-will and counter-current… But what am I doing, my friends? Of whom am I talking to you? Have I forgotten myself so far that I have not even told you his name? Unless you have already divined of your own accord who this questionable god and spirit is, that wishes to be praised in such a manner? For, as it happens to everyone who from childhood onward has always been on his legs, and in foreign lands, I have also encountered on my path many strange and dangerous spirits; above all, however, and again and again, the one of whom I have just spoken: in fact, no less a personage than the god Dionysus, the great equivocator and tempter, to whom, as you know, I once offered in all secrecy and reverence my first-fruits — the last, as it seems to me, who has offered a sacrifice to him, for I have found no one who could understand what I was then doing. In the meantime, however, I have learned much, far too much, about the philosophy of this god, and, as I said, from mouth to mouth — I, the last disciple and initiate of the god Dionysus: and perhaps I might at last begin to give you, my friends, as far as I am allowed, a little taste of this philosophy? In a hushed voice, as is but seemly: for it has to do with much that is secret, new, strange, wonderful, and uncanny. The very fact that Dionysus is a philosopher, and that therefore gods also philosophize, seems to me a novelty which is not unensnaring, and which might perhaps arouse suspicion precisely among philosophers — among you, my friends, there is less to be said against it, except that it comes too late and not at the right time; for, as has been disclosed to me, you are loath nowadays to believe in God and gods. It may happen, too, that in the frankness of my story I must go further than is agreeable to the strict usages of your ears. Certainly the god in question went further, very much further, in such dialogues, and was always many paces ahead of me… Indeed, if it were allowed, I should have to give him, according to human usage, fine ceremonious titles of lustre and merit; I should have to extol his courage as investigator and discoverer, his fearless honesty, truthfulness, and love of wisdom. But such a god does not know what to do with all that respectable trumpery and pomp. "Keep that," he would say, "for thyself and those like thee, and whoever else requires it! I — have no reason to cover my nakedness!" One suspects that this kind of divinity and philosopher perhaps lacks shame. He once said: "Under certain circumstances I love mankind" — and referred thereby to Ariadne, who was present — "in my opinion man is an agreeable, brave, inventive animal, that has not his equal upon earth; he makes his way even through all labyrinths. I like man, and often think how I can still further advance him, and make him stronger, more evil, and more profound." — "Stronger, more evil, and more profound?" I asked in horror. "Yes," he said again, "stronger, more evil, and more profound; also more beautiful" — and thereby the tempter-god smiled with his halcyon smile, as though he had just paid some charming compliment. One here sees at once that it is not only shame that this divinity lacks; and in general there are good grounds for supposing that in some things the gods could all of them come to us men for instruction. We men are — more human.

10.36.oldText: 296. Alas! what are you, after all, my written and painted thoughts! Not long ago you were so variegated, young, and malicious, so full of thorns and secret spices, that you made me sneeze and laugh — and now? You have already doffed your novelty, and some of you, I fear, are ready to become truths, so immortal do they look, so pathetically honest, so tedious! And was it ever otherwise? What then do we write and paint, we mandarins with Chinese brush, we immortalizers of things that lend themselves to writing — what are we alone capable of painting? Alas, only that which is just about to fade and begins to lose its odor! Alas, only exhausted and departing storms and belated yellow sentiments! Alas, only birds strayed and fatigued by flight, which now let themselves be captured with the hand — with our hand! We immortalize what cannot live and fly much longer — things only which are exhausted and mellow! And it is only for your afternoon, you, my written and painted thoughts, for which alone I have colors, many colors perhaps, many variegated softenings, and fifty yellows and browns and greens and reds — but nobody will divine thereby how you looked in your morning, you sudden sparks and marvels of my solitude, you, my old, beloved — evil thoughts!

11.1.oldText:
Midday of life! O season of delight!
My summer's park!
A restless joy to look, to wait, to hark —
I watch for friends, ready day and night —
Where do you linger, friends? The time is right!

11.3.oldText:
Is not the glacier's grey today, for you,
Rose-garlanded?
The brook seeks you; wind and cloud, with longing thread,
Thrust themselves higher toward the blue,
To spy you from the eagle's farthest view.

11.5.oldText:
My table was spread out for you on high —
Who dwells up here,
Star-near, so near the grisly pit below?
My realm — what realm has wider boundary?
My honey — who has sipped its fragrancy?

11.7.oldText:
Friends, you are there! Alas — yet I am not
The one you seek?
You stare and stop — better your wrath should speak!
Am I not I? Hand, gait, face — changed? And what
I am, to you my friends, now am I not?

11.9.oldText:
Have I become another? Strange to Me?
Yet sprung from Me?
A wrestler who too often wrings himself?
Too often thwarting my own soul's full reach,
Wounded and hampered by my own self-victory?

11.11.oldText:
I sought where the wind blows keenest. There
I learned to dwell
Where no man dwells, on lonesome ice-lost fell,
And unlearned man and god and curse and prayer —
Became a ghost that haunts the glaciers bare?

11.13.oldText:
You, my old friends! Look! You turn pale, filled through
With love and fear!
Go! But not in anger. You could never live here.
Here in the farthest realm of ice and scree
One must be a huntsman — must leap like chamois, free.

11.15.oldText:
An evil huntsman — was I? See how taut
My bow was bent!
Strongest was he by whom such shaft was sent —
Yet woe! That arrow is with peril fraught,
Perilous as none. — Seek the safe homes you sought!

11.17.oldText:
You go! You have endured enough, O heart —
Strong was your hope;
To new friends open wide your gates, your scope,
Let old ones be. Bid memory depart!
Were you young then? — now, better young you art!

11.19.oldText:
What once linked us together, one hope's tie —
(Who now could trace
those lines, now fading, Love once wrote thereon?) —
Is like a parchment that the hand shies by
To touch — like crackling leaves, all seared, all dry.

11.21.oldText:
Oh! Friends no more! They are — what name for those? —
Friends' phantom-flight
Knocking at my heart's window-pane at night,
Gazing at me, that speaks "We were" — and goes. —
O withered words, once fragrant as the rose!

11.23.oldText:
Yearnings of youth that could not understand!
For whom I pined,
Whom I believed were changed with me, my kind:
But they grew old, and thus were doomed and banned —
None but new kin are native of my land!

11.25.oldText:
Midday of life! My second youth's delight!
My summer's park!
A restless joy to long, to wait, to hark!
I watch for friends! — ready day and night,
For my new friends. Come! Come! The time is right!

11.29.oldText:
We keep our Feast of Feasts, sure of our bourne,
Our aims the same:
The Guest of Guests, friend Zarathustra, came!
The world now laughs, the grisly veil is torn,
And Light and Dark were one that wedding-morn.

1.0.oldText: Supposing that Truth is a woman — what then? Is there not ground for suspecting that all philosophers, insofar as they have been dogmatists, have failed to understand women — that the terrible seriousness and clumsy importunity with which they have usually paid their addresses to Truth have been unskilled and unseemly methods for winning a woman? Certainly she has never allowed herself to be won; and at present every kind of dogma stands with a sad and discouraged mien — if, indeed, it stands at all. There are scoffers who maintain that it has fallen, that all dogma lies on the ground — nay more, that it is at its last gasp. But to speak seriously, there are good grounds for hoping that all dogmatizing in philosophy — whatever solemn, whatever conclusive and decided airs it has assumed — may have been only a noble childishness and novice work; and probably the time is at hand when it will be understood once and again what has actually sufficed for the foundation of such imposing and absolute philosophical edifices as the dogmatists have hitherto reared. Perhaps some popular superstition of immemorial time (such as the soul-superstition, which in the form of subject- and ego-superstition has not yet ceased doing mischief); perhaps some play upon words, a deception on the part of grammar, or an audacious generalization of very restricted, very personal, very human — all-too-human — facts. The dogmatists' philosophy, it is to be hoped, was only a promise for thousands of years afterwards, as astrology was in still earlier times, in whose service probably more labor, gold, acuteness, and patience have been spent than on any actual science hitherto: we owe to it, and to its "super-terrestrial" pretensions in Asia and Egypt, the grand style of architecture. It seems that in order to inscribe themselves on the heart of humanity with everlasting claims, all great things must first wander about the earth as enormous and awe-inspiring caricatures. Dogmatic philosophy has been a caricature of this kind — for instance, the Vedanta doctrine in Asia, and Platonism in Europe. Let us not be ungrateful to it, though it must be confessed that the worst, the most tiresome, and the most dangerous of errors hitherto has been a dogmatist error — namely, Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself.
